steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a systems paper presenting BDFL, a blockchain-based decentralized federated learning system. Explain the problems with centralized FL and with decentralized FL, motivate using blockchain with auditors and reputations, summarize the design, and give the contributions and the paper organization.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Federated learning and the central aggregator
- Decentralized FL and its remaining challenges
- Blockchain, auditors and reputation
- BDFL
- Contributions and organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Federated learning and the central aggregator
  - FL: distributed ML paradigm, training across many distributed devices (mobile, IoT)
  - edge devices keep data local, train collaboratively without sharing training data -> privacy
  - models aggregated on central server = aggregator; distributes global model, clients train locally, send updates back, aggregator updates global model and redistributes
  - benefits: data privacy via decentralized training, lower communication cost (no raw data moved), lower computation cost (device resources)
  - but aggregator = single point of failure; compromised -> whole system fails; also bottleneck
- Decentralized FL and its remaining challenges
  - DFL removes central server; clients exchange updates directly with subset of others ('neighbors') via P2P
  - keep exchanging until local models converge to model reflecting all clients' data
  - improves single point of failure, trust dependencies, server bottleneck
  - challenges: malicious clients, low-quality models, lack of incentives -> reliability
  - unrealistic to assume all clients honest; false model updates possible
  - low-quality models affect high-quality neighbors, errors propagate through network
  - how to motivate data owners to participate and keep contributing
- Blockchain, auditors and reputation
  - blockchain: distributed ledger on P2P network, possible solution for security and incentives in DFL (Fig. 1)
  - trust: all participants verify transactions via provable cryptography and consensus protocol
  - each model update verified before aggregated and confirmed
  - storing all model updates on chain infeasible: storage and computation costs; latency, limited block size and transaction size
  - so: auditor committee + reputation mechanism; auditors manage reputations by update quality; only reputations on chain, updated periodically
- BDFL
  - Blockchain-based Decentralized Federated Learning with incentive mechanism and reputation model
  - auditors verify models; honest clients rewarded, malicious punished
  - reputation scores assigned by auditors from verification results, updated periodically
  - higher reputation -> updates more likely accepted by neighbors -> more profit
- Contributions and organization
  - first blockchain-based fully decentralized FL system for model verification, high accuracy and robustness
  - BDFL protocol suite: incentive mechanism + reputation model against malicious updates
  - evaluation on real ML datasets: high accuracy, fast convergence, resilient to client dynamics and malicious updates
  - Section II system overview/model, III protocol overview, IV detailed design, V evaluation, VI related work, VII conclusion

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Federated Learning (FL) is a distributed machine learning (ML) paradigm where ML models are trained across a lot of distributed devices, such as mobile and IoT devices. These edge devices keep their data locally and do the training tasks together without sharing the training data directly with each other, so that privacy is ensured. The trained ML models are then aggregated on a central server, which is called the aggregator. First the aggregator distributes a global model to the clients. Each client trains the model locally with its own data and generates a model update, and the update is sent back to the aggregator. The aggregator aggregates these updates to update the global model, and then distributes it to the clients again for more training. FL preserves data privacy because model training is decentralized, it saves communication costs because raw data is not moved, and it reduces computational costs because it uses the computing resource of each device. However, because there is a centralized aggregator, FL is vulnerable to a single point of failure. If the centralized aggregator is compromised, the whole FL system fails. Also, the aggregator exchanges models with clients frequently and it can become the bottleneck of the system.

Decentralized federated learning (DFL) was proposed recently and it solves these problems by removing the central server. In a DFL system, clients do not communicate with a central aggregator, but exchange model updates directly with a subset of other clients, which are called their "neighbors", using P2P communication. Clients keep exchanging model updates until their local models converge to a model that reflects the features of the data from all clients. So DFL improves on the limitations of traditional FL, which are the single point of failure, trust dependencies, and bottlenecks on the server side. But DFL still has some challenges, such as malicious clients, low-quality models, and the lack of incentives, and these undermine the reliability of the whole system. There are a large number of participants in a DFL system, so it is unrealistic to just assume that all clients are honest and follow the protocols to do the training correctly. So there may be malicious clients that share false model updates about their local training results. Also, clients with low-quality models might affect the performance of their neighbors that have high-quality models, and these errors can be propagated further in the whole network. Besides that, it is still a challenge how to motivate data owners to join the system and keep contributing their data to the FL model.

  - trust: all participants verify transactions via provable cryptography and consensus protocol
  - each model update verified before aggregated and confirmed
  - storing all model updates on chain infeasible: storage and computation costs; latency, limited block size and transaction size

- BDFL
  - Blockchain-based Decentralized Federated Learning with incentive mechanism and reputation model
  - auditors verify models; honest clients rewarded, malicious punished
  - reputation scores assigned by auditors from verification results, updated periodically
  - higher reputation -> updates more likely accepted by neighbors -> more profit

  - first blockchain-based fully decentralized FL system for model verification, high accuracy and robustness
  - BDFL protocol suite: incentive mechanism + reputation model against malicious updates

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Federated Learning (FL) is a distributed machine learning (ML) paradigm where ML models are trained across a lot of distributed devices, such as mobile and IoT devices. These edge devices keep their data locally and do the training tasks together without sharing the training data directly with each other, so that privacy is ensured. The trained ML models are then aggregated on a central server, which is called the aggregator. First the aggregator distributes a global model to the clients. Each client trains the model locally with its own data and generates a model update, and the update is sent back to the aggregator. The aggregator aggregates these updates to update the global model, and then distributes it to the clients again for more training. FL preserves data privacy because model training is decentralized, it saves communication costs because raw data is not moved, and it reduces computational costs because it uses the computing resource of each device. However, because there is a centralized aggregator, FL is vulnerable to a single point of failure. If the centralized aggregator is compromised, the whole FL system fails. Also, the aggregator exchanges models with clients frequently and it can become the bottleneck of the system.

Decentralized federated learning (DFL) was proposed recently and it solves these problems by removing the central server. In a DFL system, clients do not communicate with a central aggregator, but exchange model updates directly with a subset of other clients, which are called their "neighbors", using P2P communication. Clients keep exchanging model updates until their local models converge to a model that reflects the features of the data from all clients. So DFL improves on the limitations of traditional FL, which are the single point of failure, trust dependencies, and bottlenecks on the server side. But DFL still has some challenges, such as malicious clients, low-quality models, and the lack of incentives, and these undermine the reliability of the whole system. There are a large number of participants in a DFL system, so it is unrealistic to just assume that all clients are honest and follow the protocols to do the training correctly. So there may be malicious clients that share false model updates about their local training results. Also, clients with low-quality models might affect the performance of their neighbors that have high-quality models, and these errors can be propagated further in the whole network. Besides that, it is still a challenge how to motivate data owners to join the system and keep contributing their data to the FL model.

Blockchain is a distributed ledger technology built on a peer-to-peer network, and it is a possible solution for the security and incentive issue in the DFL system, as shown in Fig. 1. It provides trust because all participants can verify the transactions submitted to the blockchain, using its underlying provable cryptography and consensus protocol. Every participant could verify each model update before it is aggregated and confirmed in the blockchain. However, it is not feasible to directly store all model updates on the blockchain, because data storage and computation cost a lot. Pushing large model data to the blockchain also has the problem of heavy latency, limited block size, and transaction size. So we introduce an auditor committee and a reputation mechanism for model verification. Auditors manage the clients' reputations according to the quality of their model updates. Auditors do not put models or gradients on the blockchain, only the clients' reputations, and they update them periodically.

In this paper, we introduce BDFL, a Blockchain-based Decentralized Federated Learning system with an incentive mechanism and a reputation model. We introduce a set of auditors to verify models, and honest clients can get incentives while clients that provide malicious models get punished. In our reputation model, auditors assign reputation scores to clients according to the results of verifying their models, and the scores are updated periodically. If a client has a higher reputation, its model updates have a higher probability of being accepted by neighbors, so it gains more profit from the system.

To summarize, this paper makes these contributions:

- We design BDFL, which is the first blockchain-based fully decentralized federated learning system for model verification, with high learning accuracy and system robustness.

- We design and implement the BDFL protocol suite. We introduce an incentive mechanism that encourages clients to participate in model exchange, and a reputation model that evaluates how trustworthy each client is, to avoid malicious model updates from attackers.

- We evaluate BDFL with experiments on real ML datasets. BDFL achieves high model accuracy and fast convergence, and it is strongly resilient to client dynamics and malicious model updates.

The rest of the paper is organized like this. Section II presents the system overview and model. Section III describes a protocol overview and Section IV the detailed design of BDFL. Section V presents the evaluation results of our protocol. Section VI describes the related work, and Section VII concludes.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Federated Learning (FL) [1] is a distributed machine learning (ML) paradigm that allows training ML models across numerous distributed devices, such as mobile and IoT devices. These edge devices hold their data locally and collaboratively perform training tasks without directly sharing training data among them, which ensures privacy. The trained ML models are then aggregated on a central server, called the aggregator. The aggregator first distributes a global model to clients. Each client trains the model locally using its own data and generates a model update, which is sent back to the aggregator. The aggregator aggregates these updates to update the global model, and distributes it to clients for further training. FL preserves data privacy by enabling decentralized model training [2,3], saves communication costs by avoiding moving raw data, and reduces computational costs by leveraging the computing resources of each device. However, the existence of the centralized aggregator makes FL vulnerable to a single point of failure [4]. Once the centralized aggregator is compromised, the whole FL system fails. Also, since the aggregator frequently exchanges models with clients, it can become the bottleneck of the system.

The recently proposed concept of decentralized federated learning (DFL) [5,6,7,8] solves these problems by removing the central server. In a DFL system, instead of communicating with a central aggregator, clients directly exchange model updates with a subset of other clients, known as their "neighbors", using P2P communication. Clients keep exchanging model updates until their local models converge to a model that reflects the features of data from all clients. Thus, DFL addresses the single point of failure, trust dependencies, and server-side bottlenecks of traditional FL. However, DFL still faces challenges such as malicious clients, low-quality models, and the lack of incentives, which undermine the reliability of the whole system. Given the large number of participants in a DFL system, it is unrealistic to simply assume that all clients are honest and follow the protocols to train correctly. Malicious clients may therefore share false model updates about their local training results. Also, clients with low-quality models might affect the performance of their neighbors with high-quality models, and these errors may be further propagated through the whole network. Besides, how to motivate data owners to participate in the system and continuously contribute their data to the FL model remains a challenge.

Blockchain, a distributed ledger technology built on a peer-to-peer network, provides a possible solution for the security and incentive issues in DFL systems [9], as shown in Fig. 1. It provides trust by allowing all participants to verify transactions submitted to the blockchain through its underlying provable cryptography and consensus protocol. Every participant could verify each model update before it is aggregated and confirmed in the blockchain. However, directly storing all model updates on the blockchain is not feasible due to the significant costs of data storage and computation, and pushing large model data to the blockchain suffers from heavy latency and limited block and transaction sizes. We therefore introduce an auditor committee and a reputation mechanism for model verification. Auditors are responsible for managing clients' reputations according to the quality of their model updates. Instead of models or gradients, auditors only put clients' reputations on the blockchain and update them periodically.

In this paper, we introduce BDFL, a Blockchain-based Decentralized Federated Learning system with an incentive mechanism and a reputation model. We introduce a set of auditors for model verification: honest clients receive incentives, while clients providing malicious models are punished. In our reputation model, clients' reputation scores are assigned by auditors according to their model verification results and updated periodically. Clients with higher reputations have a higher probability of their model updates being accepted by neighbors, and thus gain more profit from the system.

In summary, this paper makes the following contributions:

- • We design BDFL, the first blockchain-based fully decentralized federated learning system for model verification with high learning accuracy and system robustness.

- • We design and implement the BDFL protocol suite. We introduce an incentive mechanism to encourage clients to participate in model exchange, and a reputation model to evaluate the trustworthiness of each client and avoid malicious model updates from attackers.

- • We evaluate BDFL with experiments on real ML datasets. BDFL achieves high model accuracy and fast convergence, and is strongly resilient to client dynamics and malicious model updates.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the system overview and model. Section III gives a protocol overview and Section IV the detailed design of BDFL. Section V presents the evaluation results of our protocol. Section VI describes related work, and Section VII concludes this work.

References:

[2] C. Ma, J. Li, M. Ding, H. H. Yang, F. Shu, T. Q. Quek, and H. V. Poor, “On safeguarding privacy and security in the framework of federated learning,” IEEE network , 2020.

[4] T. Li, A. K. Sahu, A. Talwalkar, and V. Smith, “Federated learning: Challenges, methods, and future directions,” IEEE signal processing magazine , 2020.
